source_text: Verum quid nos tam obstipe veritatis solius rationem sequendam putamus; cum inimicorum nostrorum phalanx ipsis innitatur rerum periculis, et insurgat in nos aerumnarum munita suffragiis? Vult quippe pudore coeuntis, dolore parientis, sudore laborantis, transmissionem culparum et poenarum in semina comprobare; ut his videlicet signis, difficilium partuum, agricolarum sudantium, et dumosorum novalium, crimen naturale credatur, cuius merito per tot incommoda genus exerceatur humanum; quod quidam per Adae peccatum, mortale opinantur effectum. Ideo autem dixi: Quidam, quia princeps eorum Augustinus hoc quidem erubuit dicere. Denique scribit ad Marcellinum, mortalem Adam factum videri; sed elegantia solita subdit, mortem stipendium iniquitatis fuisse; et quem fatetur mortaliter institutum secundum naturam, mori non potuisse pronuntiat. Illae ergo adversus nos, quae leguntur in Genesi, sententiae proferri solent, quibus Adam atque Eva vexantur, de quibus disserendi iam est tempus. Dixit - inquit - Dominus Deus serpenti: Quia fecisti hoc, maledictus tu ab omnibus pecoribus, et ab omnibus bestiis quae sunt super terram; super pectus et ventrem ambulabis, et terram manducabis omnibus diebus vitae tuae; et inimicitias ponam inter te et mulierem, et inter semen tuum et semen eius. Ipsa tuum captabit caput, et tu illius captabis calcaneum. Mulieri vero dixit: Multiplicans multiplicabo tristitias tuas et gemitum tuum; in tristitia paries filios, et ad virum tuum conversio tua, et ipse tui dominabitur. Adae autem dixit: Quoniam audisti vocem mulieris tuae, et manducasti de ligno, de quo praeceperam tibi de eo solo ne manducares ex eo, maledicta terra in operibus tuis; in tristitia manducabis eam omnibus diebus vitae tuae; spinas et tribulos edet tibi, et edes fenum agri tui; in sudore faciei tuae edes panem tuum, donec convertaris in terram de qua sumptus es; quoniam terra es, et in terram ibis [n153] . Has ergo sententias ad testimonium ingenitae iniquitatis assumitis, concionaminique non fuisse in pariendo feminas dolituras, nisi ad eas cum peccato Evae fecunditatis illius aerumna transisset. Ipsum ergo supplicium vultis esse peccati indicium, ut quod prima feminarum meruit per delictum, nulla quoque sine eadem credatur iniquitate sentire. Non enim esset, inquitis, dolor in pariente, nisi in nascente esset peccatum. His ergo quam attonitus occurram, haud facile metior? Tantum enim stimulorum admovit in hoc loco vestra opinio, ut vix digner ad certationem moveri; plura quippe in his obiectionibus intellegentiae sunt peccata quam syllabae.
pass_a_gloss: But why do we so stubbornly think the reason of truth alone must be followed; when the phalanx of our enemies leans on the very dangers of things, and rises against us fortified by the suffrages of hardships? For he wants by the shame of one coupling, the pain of one giving birth, the sweat of one laboring, to prove a transmission of faults and of penalties into seeds; so that namely by these signs, of difficult births, of sweating farmers, and of bushy fallows, a natural charge is believed, by whose desert the human race is exercised through so many inconveniences; which certain people opine was made mortal through Adam's sin. But therefore I said: Certain people, because their prince Augustine blushed indeed to say this. Finally he writes to Marcellinus, that Adam seems made mortal; but with the usual elegance he subjoins that death was a wage of iniquity; and him whom he confesses instituted mortally according to nature, he pronounces could not die. Those sentences therefore against us, which are read in Genesis, are accustomed to be brought forth, by which Adam and Eve are vexed, about which it is now time of discussing. The Lord God, it says, said to the serpent: Because you did this, cursed are you from all cattle, and from all beasts which are upon the earth; upon breast and belly you will walk, and you will eat earth all the days of your life; and I will place enmities between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. She will catch your head, and you will catch her heel. But to the woman he said: Multiplying I will multiply your sadnesses and your groan; in sadness you will bear sons, and your turning is to your husband, and he will lord it over you. But to Adam he said: Because you heard the voice of your woman, and you ate from the tree, about which I had precepted you from it alone that you not eat from it, cursed is the earth in your works; in sadness you will eat it all the days of your life; it will eat out thorns and thistles for you, and you will eat the hay of your field; in the sweat of your face you will eat your bread, until you are turned into the earth from which you were taken; because you are earth, and into earth you will go. These sentences therefore you take up for a testimony of inborn iniquity, and you harangue that females would not have been about to grieve in giving birth, unless to them with Eve's sin the hardship of that fertility had passed. You therefore want the punishment itself to be an indication of sin, so that what the first of females deserved through an offense, none also is believed to feel without the same iniquity. For there would not be, you say, pain in the one giving birth, unless there were sin in the one being born. To these therefore how astonished I would meet, I do not easily measure? For so many goads did your opinion apply in this place, that I scarcely deign to be moved to contestation; for there are more sins of understanding in these objections than syllables.

pass_b_english: But why do we stubbornly think only truth’s reasoning should be followed, when our enemies’ battle line relies on the very dangers of life and rises against us fortified by miseries’ support? It wants to prove the transmission of faults and punishments into reproductive seed through the shame of intercourse, the pain of childbirth, and the sweat of labor. These signs—difficult births, sweating farmers, and thorny fields—are meant to make us believe in a natural crime for which the human race is exercised by so many troubles. Some think Adam’s sin made the race mortal.

I said ‘some’ because their leader Augustine was ashamed to say this. Writing to Marcellinus, he says Adam appears to have been made mortal. Yet with his usual elegance he adds that death was the wages of iniquity (compare Romans 6:23), and pronounces that the one he admits was established mortal according to nature could not have died. Those pronouncements in Genesis which afflict Adam and Eve are therefore commonly brought against us. It is now time to discuss them.

‘The Lord God said to the serpent: Because you have done this, you are cursed beyond all cattle and all beasts upon the earth. You shall go upon your breast and belly and eat earth all the days of your life. I will put enmity between you and the woman, between your seed and her seed. She shall watch for your head, and you shall watch for her heel.
‘To the woman he said: I will greatly multiply your sorrows and your groaning. In sorrow you shall bear children; your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you.

‘To Adam he said: Because you listened to your wife’s voice and ate from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat from that one alone, the earth is cursed in your works. In sorrow you shall eat from it all the days of your life. It shall produce thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the grass of your field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread until you return to the earth from which you were taken, because you are earth, and into earth you shall go’ (Genesis 3:14–19).

You take these pronouncements as evidence of inborn iniquity and proclaim that women would not have suffered pain in childbirth unless the misery of Eve’s childbearing had passed to them along with her sin. You want the punishment itself to prove sin, so that what the first woman earned through her offense cannot be felt by any woman without the same iniquity. ‘There would be no pain in the woman giving birth,’ you say, ‘unless there were sin in the child being born.’

I can scarcely measure how astonished I am in meeting these claims. Your opinion has supplied so many irritations here that I can scarcely bring myself to contest it. These objections contain more sins against understanding than syllables.
